Surah 75: Al-Qiyamah (The Resurrection)
Forty verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾. In this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: the exegetes have mentioned three views regarding the particle "﴿lā﴾" in His words "﴿lā uqsimu﴾":

The first: it is an extra, superfluous particle (ṣila zā'ida), and the meaning is "I swear by the Day of Resurrection." Its parallels are ﴿li-allā yaʿlama ahl al-kitāb﴾ [al-Hadid: 29] and His words ﴿mā manaʿaka allā tasjud﴾ and ﴿fa-bimā raḥmatin mina Allāh﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. However, this view is, in my opinion, weak for several reasons:

First: permitting this leads to casting doubt on the Qur'an, because on this assumption it would be permissible to turn negation into affirmation and affirmation into negation, and permitting that would mean that no reliance could be placed either on its affirmation or on its negation.

Second: this particle is used in the middle of a speech, not at its beginning. If it is said: the discussion on this has two sides:

The first: we do not concede that it is used only in the middle of speech. Do you not see how Imru' al-Qays used it at the opening of his qasida, where he says:

"No, by your father, daughter of al-'Amiri, the people do not claim that I flee."

The second: suppose this particle is not used at the beginning of speech, yet the whole Qur'an is like a single surah, because its parts are connected to one another. The proof is that a matter may be mentioned in one surah and its answer come in another surah, such as His saying: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, indeed you are mad"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], then its answer came in another surah: ﴿You are not, by the favour of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam: 2]. If that is so, the beginning of this surah is treated like the middle of speech.

The answer to the first: his saying "lā wa-abīki" is an oath with negation, whereas His saying ﴿lā uqsimu﴾ is a negation of the oath. So likening one to the other is not permissible. We said that His saying ﴿lā uqsimu﴾ is a negation of the oath because it is on the pattern of our saying: "lā aqtulu, lā aḍribu, lā anṣuru" (I do not kill, I do not strike, I do not help), and it is known that this conveys negation. The proof of this is that if someone swears "I will not swear," then fulfilling (the oath) (barr) is by abstaining from swearing, and breaking it (ḥinth) is by performing the oath. Thus it is evident that the mentioned verse

is not of this category.

As for the second: the Qur'an is like a single surah in not being contradictory. Now, either every verse must be accompanied by what accompanies the other verse, which is impermissible, because it would entail that the negative particle could be attached to every affirmation in the other verses, and that requires every affirmation becoming a negation and every negation becoming an affirmation, and that is not permissible.

Third: what we mean by "lā" being a superfluous particle is vain and false; it must be discarded and dropped so that the speech may be coherent, and it is known that describing the speech of God Most High in this way is not permissible.

The second view of the exegetes on this verse: it is reported from al-Hasan that he read "la-uqsimu" (with a lām), taking the lām as the lām of inception (lam al-ibtida'), and "uqsimu" as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "Indeed I, I swear." It is supported by its being written without an alif in the Codex of 'Uthman, and they agreed on His words ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾ as "lā uqsimu." Al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is that I swear by the Day of Resurrection because of its nobility, and I do not swear by the self-reproaching soul because of its baseness. Abu 'Ubayda criticised this reading and said: had this been the meaning, it would have said "la-uqsimanna" (with the emphatic nun), because the Arabs do not say "la-af'alu kadha" but say "la-af'alanna kadha." However, al-Wahidi related the permissibility of this from Sibawayh and al-Farra'. Know that this view too is weak, because this reading is anomalous (shadhdhah). Suppose this anomalous reading persisted: what is the position regarding the well-known, mutawatir reading? It cannot be dismissed, otherwise that would be a discrediting of what is established by mass transmission. Moreover, it would be necessary to posit another oath, so that this lām would be the answer to it, and the sense would become: "By God, I swear by the Day of Resurrection," making it an oath upon an oath, which is weak, and it leads to an infinite regress (tasalsul).

The third view: the word "lā" came as a negation. There are then two possibilities:

The first: it came as a negation of a statement mentioned before the oath, as if they had denied resurrection, so it was said: "No, the matter is not as you have claimed," and then it was said: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection." This too has a difficulty, because repeating the negative particle again in His words ﴿and I swear by the self-reproaching soul﴾, while the intended meaning is what they mentioned, detracts from the eloquence of the speech.

The second possibility: "lā" here negates the oath, as if He said: "I do not swear to you by that day and that soul, but I ask you without swearing: do you think that We will not gather your bones when they are scattered by death? If you think so, know that We are able to do that." This view is the choice of Abu Muslim, and it is the most correct. This view can be explained in several other ways:

One: as if He, Most High, says: "I do not swear by these things to establish this matter, for this matter is greater and more majestic than to be sworn to by these things," and the purpose of this speech is to glorify what is sworn to and to magnify its status.

Second: as if He, Most High, says: "I do not swear by these things to establish this matter, for its establishment is more evident, clearer, stronger and more fitting than that one should attempt to establish it by such an oath." Then He said after it: ﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾, i.e., how did this corrupt thought occur to his mind despite the evidence of its corruption?

Third: the purpose may be interrogation in the manner of denial, the sense being: "Shall I not swear by the Day of Resurrection? Shall I not swear by the self-reproaching soul that resurrection and gathering are true?"

The second issue: they have mentioned several views concerning "the self-reproaching soul" (al-nafs al-lawwamah):

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: every soul will blame itself on the Day of Resurrection, whether it was righteous or wicked. As for the righteous, it is because it did not increase in its obedience; as for the wicked, it is because why did it not occupy itself with piety. Some critics objected to this view on several grounds:

First: one who deserves reward may not blame himself for failing to increase (his good deeds), because if it were permissible for him to blame himself for that, it would be permissible for others to blame him for it.

Second: a person blames himself only in distress and constriction of the heart, and that does not befit the people of Paradise while they are in Paradise. Moreover, the responsible person knows that there is no amount of obedience but that something greater than it can be done; so if that were the cause of blame, it would be impossible to be free of it, and what is like that is not something sought to be attained, nor is one blamed for not attaining it. The answer to all of this: the blame should be understood as wishing for more, and then these objections fall away.

Second: the self-reproaching soul is the pious souls which blame the disobedient soul on the Day of Resurrection because it abandoned piety.

Third: they are the noble souls which never cease to blame themselves however diligent they are in obedience. It is related from al-Hasan that the believer is never seen but blaming himself, whereas the ignorant one is content with the base state he is in.

Fourth: it is the soul of Adam, which never ceased to blame itself for the act by which it left Paradise.

Fifth: the intended meaning is the souls of the wretched when they witness the conditions and terrors of the Resurrection, for they blame themselves for the sins they committed. A parallel is His words: ﴿lest a soul say, "Alas for my regret over what I neglected"﴾ [al-Zumar: 56].

Sixth: man was created restless (malūlan), so whatever he seeks, when he obtains it he becomes weary of it, and then he blames himself, saying, "Why did I seek it?" Because this act is frequent, he is called the self-reproaching soul. A parallel is His words: ﴿Indeed man was created anxious; when evil touches him he is distressed, and when good touches him he is withholding﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19–21]. Know that the word "lawwamah" (intensive form) indicates repetition and recurrence, and the same is said of "lawwam," "'adhdhab," and "darrar."

The third issue: know that the verse contains several difficulties:

One: what is the connection between the Resurrection and the self-reproaching soul, such that God joined them together in the oath?

Two: the thing sworn to is the occurrence of the Resurrection, so the result becomes that He swore by the occurrence of the Resurrection.

Three: why did He say ﴿lā uqsimu bi-yawmi al-qiyamah﴾ and not "wa-al-qiyamah," as He said in the other surahs: "wa-al-ṭūr," "wa-al-dhāriyāt," "wa-al-ḍuḥā"?

As for the first question, the answer has several aspects:

One: the conditions of the Resurrection are extremely wondrous, and the purpose of establishing the Resurrection is to manifest the conditions of the self-reproaching souls, I mean their felicity and wretchedness; thus this strong connection has come about between the Resurrection and the self-reproaching souls.

Two: swearing by the self-reproaching soul is an alert to the wondrous conditions of the soul, as he, upon whom be peace, said: "Whoever knows himself knows his Lord." Among its wondrous conditions is His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], and His saying: ﴿Indeed We offered the trust…and man bore it﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. Some said: the oath was sworn by the self-reproaching soul to express its glorification, in that it always belittles its own action and its striving in obedience to God. Others said: He swore by the Resurrection and did not swear by the self-reproaching soul, and this is on the anomalous reading we have related from al-Hasan: it is as if He said: "I swear by the Day of Resurrection" to glorify it, and "I do not swear by the soul" to belittle it, because the self-reproaching soul is either disbelieving in the Resurrection despite its great importance, or it is wicked and negligent in action; and in either case it is deserving of contempt.

As for the second question, the answer to it is what we mentioned: the verification scholars said that swearing by these things is in reality swearing by their Lord and Creator, as if it were said: "I swear by the Lord of the Resurrection that the Day of Resurrection will occur."

As for the third question, its answer is that where He swore, He said: ﴿wa-al-ṭūr﴾, ﴿wa-al-dhāriyāt﴾; but here He negated that He was swearing by these things, so the question falls away. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 75, verses 3–4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: They have mentioned several views regarding the answer to the oath.

The first of them, which is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur), is that it is elided, the implied meaning being "He will surely be resurrected" (la-yub'athanna), and what indicates it is ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾.

The second: al-Hasan said: the oath falls upon His saying, ﴿Yes, [We are] able﴾.

The third, and it is the closest, is that this is not an oath at all but a negation of an oath, so it does not need an answer. It is as if He, exalted is He, were saying: I do not swear by such-and-such for anything; rather, I ask you: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾.

The second issue: The well-known view is that by "man" (al-insan) is meant a specific individual. It is related that ʿAdi ibn Abi Rabiʿa, the brother-in-law of al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and they are the two of whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "O Allah, suffice me against the evil of my bad neighbours," said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, tell me about the Day of Resurrection: when will it be and what is its matter?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed him, and he said: "Even if I witnessed that day, I would not believe you, O Muhammad, nor would I have faith in you. How will Allah gather the bones?" Then this verse was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: by "man" here he means Abu Jahl. A group of the scholars of usul (al-Usuliyyun) said: rather, the intended meaning of "man" is the one who denies resurrection in general.

The third issue: Qatada recited: "An lan tujmaʿa ʿizamuhu" in the passive form, and the meaning is that the disbeliever thought that the bones, after they have scattered and become dust, and those parts have mixed with others, and after the winds have blown them away and scattered them in the distant parts of the earth, cannot be gathered again. And He, exalted is He, said in reply: ﴿Yes﴾. This word makes obligatory what follows the negation, which is the gathering; it is as if it were said: "Rather, He will gather them." Regarding His saying ﴿able﴾ there are two aspects:

The first, which is the well-known one, is that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "najmaʿu" (We gather), meaning: We gather the bones, being able to assemble them all and return them to their original formation. However, this aspect is problematic in my view, because a circumstantial clause is appropriately mentioned only when the matter could occur without that state; you say "I saw Zayd riding," because it is possible to see Zayd not riding. Here, His, exalted is He, gathering the bones is impossible to occur except with His being able, so making it a circumstantial clause would be like explaining the obvious, and this is not permissible.

The second: the sense of the verse is: "We were able to put together his fingertips at the beginning, so it is necessary that We remain able to make that arrangement at the end." It was also read "qadirun" (We are able). Regarding His saying ﴿to put together his fingertips﴾ there are several aspects:

The first: He drew attention with the fingertips to the rest of the limbs, meaning: We are able to put his fingertips back together after they have become dust as they were. The verification of this is that whoever is able to do a thing at the beginning is also able to do it in the restoration. The fingertips were singled out for mention because they are the last part of the body to be completed in creation. It is as if it were said: We are able to join its small and delicate joints, some to others, as they were at first, without deficiency or disparity; so how much more so the large bones.

The second: ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together his fingertips﴾, meaning: We make them, together with his palm, a smooth flat surface with no creases, like the foot of a camel, so that the benefit of delicate works such as writing, sewing and all the other delicate works for which the fingers are used is lost. The first view is closer to the correct one.

The second: that what is meant is his limbs, which bear witness against him for what he did; so he is a witness against himself through the testimony of his limbs. ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: some of the early Rafidis claimed that this Qur'an has been altered, changed, added to and reduced. They argued for this by saying that there is no connection between this verse and what precedes it, and if this arrangement were from God Most High, the matter would not be so.

Know that there are several aspects to explaining the connection:

The first of them: it is possible that the hastening that was forbidden occurred to the Messenger, peace be upon him, at the time of the revelation of these verses to him, so he was forbidden from that hastening at this time, and it was said to him: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾. This is like a teacher who is dictating something to his student, and the student begins to look right and left, so the teacher says during that lesson: Do not look right and left, and then returns to the lesson. When that lesson is transmitted together with this remark within it, whoever does not know the cause will say: the occurrence of that word in the middle of that lesson is not appropriate; but whoever knows the incident knows that the arrangement is good.

The second: He, Exalted is He, related of the disbelievers that they love the hasty worldly happiness, and that is His saying: ﴿Nay, man desires to continue in sin before him﴾. Then He explained that hastening is blameworthy absolutely, even hastening in matters of religion, so He said: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾, and He said at the end of the verse: ﴿Nay, but you love the hasty [life]﴾.

It was as if it was said to him: if you offer this excuse, yet you know that memorization is not achieved except by God's grant and help, then leave this hastening and rely on the guidance of God Most High. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾.

The first issue: the word ʿalā (upon) indicates obligation, so His saying: ﴿Indeed, upon Us﴾ shows that this is as if obligatory upon God Most High. According to our school, this obligation is by the rule of promise. According to the Mu'tazilah, it is because the purpose of the prophethood is not completed unless the revelation is preserved and protected from forgetfulness, so this is obligatory in view of wisdom.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 75, verse 19–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: The verse indicates that he (peace be upon him) used to recite along with the recitation of Jibril (peace be upon him), and he would ask during his recitation about its difficulties and its meanings, out of his eagerness for knowledge. So the Prophet (peace be upon him) was forbidden from both matters together. As for reciting along with the recitation of Jibril, it is by His saying: ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾. As for asking questions during the explanation, it is by His saying: ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾.

The second issue: Whoever permits delaying the explanation (bayan) past the time of address (waqt al-khitab) has argued with this verse.

Abu al-Husayn (al-Basri) answered it in two ways:

The first: The apparent meaning of the verse requires that the delaying of the explanation past the time of address is obligatory, and you (the Ash'aris) do not say this.

The second: According to us, what is obligatory is that the utterance be accompanied by an indication that the intended meaning of the utterance is not what its apparent meaning requires. As for detailed explanation (al-bayan al-tafsili), its delay is permissible. So the verse is to be understood as referring to the delay of detailed explanation. Al-Qaffal mentioned a third answer: that His saying ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾ means: "Then indeed We inform you that upon Us is its explanation." A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path. And what can make you know what the steep path is? It is the freeing of a slave... and then he is of those who believed﴾ [Al-Balad: 11–17].

As for the answer to the first: The wording does not require the obligation of delaying the explanation, but rather requires the delay of the obligation of explanation, and according to us the matter is so, because the obligation of explanation is not realized except at the time of need.

As for the answer to the second: The word "thumma" (then) entered upon the absolute explanation, so it includes both the summary (mujmal) and the detailed (mufassal) explanation. As for al-Qaffal's objection, it is also weak, because it abandons the apparent meaning without evidence.

The third issue: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then indeed upon Us is its explanation﴾ indicates that the explanation of what is summary (mujmal) is obligatory upon Allah, may He be exalted. As for us, it is by promise and grace (tafaddul). As for the Mu'tazilah, it is by wisdom (hikmah).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, but you love the immediate﴾ ﴿and leave the Hereafter﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "﴿Nay﴾ is a restraint of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) from the habit of hastiness, and an urging toward deliberation and gravity. He has emphasized this by following it with His saying: ﴿but you love the immediate﴾, as if He said: 'Rather, you, O children of Adam, because you were created from haste and were disposed to it, you hasten in everything, and for this reason you love the immediate and leave the Hereafter.'" The rest of the commentators said: "﴿Nay﴾ means 'truly', i.e., truly you love the immediate and leave the Hereafter. The meaning is that they love this world and work for it, and leave the Hereafter and turn away from it."

The second issue: "tuhibbuna" and "tadharuna" have been read with the ta' and with the ya'. In this there are two views:

The first: Al-Farra' said: When the Qur'an descends describing the state of a people, sometimes it descends by way of direct address to them, and sometimes it descends by way of third-person reference, as in His saying: ﴿until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them﴾ [Yunus: 22].

The second: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: The ya' refers to what preceded of the mention of man in His saying: ﴿Does man think...﴾, and what is meant by it is the multitude, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, man was created anxious﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 19]. The meaning is: they love and they leave. And the ta' is as if: "Say to them: Rather, you love and you leave."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 75, verses 22–23 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant﴾. Al-Layth said: The color, the tree, and the leaf become radiant (yanduru) with radiance (nadrah). Nadrah means blessing, and nadir means one who is luxuriant. Al-nadir means the good of everything. From this it is said of a color when it is bright: nadir. So one says "green and radiant" (akhdar nadir), and likewise for all colors. Its meaning is that which has a sheen. Similarly it is said: a radiant tree (shajar nadir) and a radiant meadow (rawd nadir). From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "May God make radiant the face of a servant who hears my saying and preserves it," the hadith. Most narrators transmit it with the light (takhfif) pronunciation, while Ikrimah narrated from al-Asma'i with the emphatic (tashdid) pronunciation. The wordings of the exegetes differ in explaining al-nadir, but their meaning is one. They said: joyful (masrurah), blessed (na'imah), luminous (mudi'ah), bright (mushriqah), delighted (bahijah). Al-Zajjaj said: they are made radiant by the bliss of Paradise, as He said: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ (Al-Mutaffifin: 24).

﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾.

Know that the majority of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah, the Sunni majority) hold fast to this verse to establish that the believers will see God, exalted is He, on the Day of Resurrection. As for the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school), they have two positions here:

The first: explaining that its apparent meaning does not indicate the seeing of God, exalted is He.

The second: explaining the interpretation (ta'wil, figurative interpretation).

As for the first position, they said: the verb "nazara" (to look) when joined with the particle "ila" (toward) is not a name for seeing (ru'yah), but for the preliminary to seeing, which is turning the pupil toward the object seen, seeking to see it. The looking of the eye in relation to seeing is like the looking of the heart in relation to knowing, and like listening in relation to hearing. Just as the looking of the heart is a preliminary to knowledge, and listening is a preliminary to hearing, so the looking of the eye is a preliminary to seeing. They said: What shows that looking is not a name for seeing are several points:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you see them looking at you, while they do not see﴾ (Al-A'raf: 198). He affirmed looking in the state of not seeing, which shows that looking is other than seeing.

The second: Looking is described by things that seeing is not described by. One says: he looked at him with a sidelong glance (nazaran shazaran), he looked angrily (nazara ghadbana), he looked with approval (nazara radin). All of this is because the movement of the pupil indicates these states, whereas seeing is not described by any of that. So one does not say: he saw him sidelong, or he saw him with the seeing of an angry man, or the seeing of one who approves.

The third: One says: look at him until you see him (inzur ilayhi hatta tarahu), and: I looked at him and I saw him. This indicates that seeing is the end-goal of looking, and that requires a difference between looking and seeing.

The fourth: One says: the houses of the sons of so-and-so are mutanaziyah (facing one another), that is, mutaqabilah (opposite). So the name of looking is present here, but the name of seeing is not present.

The fifth: the saying of the poet:

Faces looking, on the Day of Badr, toward the Merciful, awaiting deliverance.

He affirmed looking with the particle "ila," although seeing was not present.

The sixth: Abu 'Ali al-Farisi argued that looking is not an expression for seeing, which is the perception of sight, but rather an expression for turning the pupil toward the direction in which the thing one wishes to see is located, citing the poet's saying:

O Mayy, will my weeping repay its like, repeatedly, and my breaths, sighing toward you?
And whenever I overlook the side where you are, among all the sides, I am looking.

He said: If looking were an expression for seeing, the lover would not seek reward for it, since the lover does not seek reward for seeing the beloved, for that is among his greatest aims. He said: What also indicates this is the saying of another:

And the glance of one with longing, passionate, when the riding camels have passed a mile.

What is meant by it is turning the pupil toward the side where the beloved is. Thus we know by these points that looking joined with the particle "ila" is not a name for seeing.

The seventh: His saying: ﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾ means that they look toward their Lord specifically and do not look toward anything else. This is the meaning of placing the object first (taqdim al-maf'ul). Do you not see His saying: ﴿Toward your Lord on that day is the place of rest﴾ (Al-Qiyamah: 12), ﴿Toward your Lord on that day is the driving﴾ (Al-Qiyamah: 30), ﴿Surely to God the affairs will return﴾ (Al-Shura: 53), ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ (Al-Zukhruf: 85), ﴿And to God is the final destination﴾ (Fatir: 18), ﴿In Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn penitent﴾ (Al-Shura: 10). How in these cases the placing first indicates the sense of exclusivity. It is known that they look at things that cannot be encompassed by enumeration and are not included in a count in the station of Resurrection. For the believers are the spectators of that Day, since they are the secure, of whom it is said: ﴿No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 62). So when the verse indicates that looking is only toward God, and reason indicates that they see other than God, we know that what is meant by looking toward God is not seeing.

The eighth: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ (Al 'Imran: 77). Had He said "will not see them," it would have sufficed. Since He negated looking and did not negate seeing, this indicates a difference. Thus it is established by these points that the looking mentioned in this verse is not seeing.

The second position: the detailed interpretation, and it is of two kinds:

The first: that "al-nazir" means "al-muntazir" (one who awaits). That is, those people await the reward of God. This is like the saying of one who says: I only look to so-and-so for my need, meaning I await its success from him. And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they will wait to see what the messengers return with﴾ (Al-Naml: 35), and He said: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then [let there be] postponement until a time of ease﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 280). It is said: looking joined with "ila" is not used in the sense of waiting. And waiting is distress and pain, which is not fitting for the people of happiness on the Day of Resurrection. We say: The answer to the first is in two parts:

The first: looking joined with the particle "ila" is sometimes used in the sense of waiting and expectation. The evidence for this is that one says: I am looking toward so-and-so to see what he will do with me, meaning expectation and hope. The poet said:

And when I look to you from a king, while the sea is beyond you, you increase my blessings.

The truth of the matter is this: when they say in waiting "nazartu" (I looked) without a complement, that is for waiting for a person to come himself. But when one is awaiting his support and aid, it may be said: "nazartu ilayhi" (I looked toward him), like the saying of a man: "My looking is only toward God, then toward you." Someone who cannot see may say this, and the blind man says in this sense: "My eye is fixed upon you." Furthermore, even if we concede that, we do not concede that "ila" here is the particle of transitivity, but rather it is the singular of "al-ala'" (blessings), and the meaning is: faces on that day radiant, awaiting the blessing of their Lord.

As for the second question, that waiting is distress and pain, its answer is that the one who waits, when he is certain of reaching what he awaits, is in the greatest of pleasures.

The second interpretation: that the object be elided (idmar al-mudaf), and the meaning is: looking toward the reward of their Lord. They said: We only went to this interpretation because when the textual and rational proofs indicated that seeing Him, exalted is He, is impossible, it became necessary to resort to interpretation. And one might say: This verse also indicates that looking is not an expression for turning the pupil, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will not look at them﴾, and it is not meant that He turns the pupil toward Hell. If you say: What is meant is that He will not look at them with a look of mercy, that would be our answer to what they have said.

The third interpretation: that the meaning of ﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾ is that they do not ask or desire except from God. This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Worship God as if you see Him." So the people of the Resurrection, because of their intense supplication to Him and the severing of their hopes from anything else, become as if they are looking at Him. The answer: His saying: "Looking is not an expression for seeing." We say: Here there are two positions:

The first: to establish the proof that looking is seeing, in two ways:

The first: what God, exalted is He, related about Moses, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Show me [Yourself], that I may look at You﴾ (Al-A'raf: 143). If looking were an expression for turning the pupil toward the direction of the object seen, the verse would imply that Moses, peace be upon him, attributed to God, exalted is He, a direction and a place, and that is impossible.

The second: that He made looking something dependent upon desire (al-irada), so looking comes after desire. Turning the pupil does not come after desire, so it must be that looking is an expression for turning the pupil toward the direction of the object seen.

* * *

The second position, which is closer to the correct: Granting that looking is an expression for turning the pupil toward the object seen seeking to see it, we still say: since it is impossible to take it in its literal sense, it must be taken as referring to its cause, which is seeing, by using the name of the cause for the effect. Taking it to mean seeing is better than taking it to mean waiting, because turning the pupil is like a cause of seeing, and there is no connection between it and waiting. So taking it to mean seeing is better than taking it to mean waiting.

As for his saying that looking has come in the sense of waiting, we say: we have two positions in answer:

The first: that looking in the sense of waiting occurs frequently in the Qur'an, but it was never joined at all with the particle "ila," such as His saying: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾ (Al-Hadid: 13), and His saying: ﴿Do they await except its interpretation?﴾ (Al-A'raf: 53), ﴿Do they await except that God come to them?﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 210). What we claim is that looking joined with the particle "ila" and transitive to faces is nothing but in the sense of seeing or in the sense that results in seeing, which is evident. Therefore it must not occur in the sense of waiting, in order to avoid homonymy.

As for the saying of the poet:

Faces looking, on the Day of Badr, toward the Merciful, awaiting deliverance.

We say: this verse is fabricated, and the correct transmission is:

Faces looking, on the Day of Bakr, toward the Merciful, awaiting deliverance.

What is meant by this "Merciful" is Musaylimah the Liar, for they used to call him "the Merciful of Yamamah." So his companions were looking at him and expecting from him deliverance from the enemies.

As for the poet's saying:

And when I look to you from a king,

the answer is that his saying "and when I look to you" cannot mean waiting, because mere waiting does not result in a gift. Rather, what is meant by his saying "and when I look to you" is "and when I ask you," because looking at a person is the prelude to conversation, so it is permissible to express it by that. As for his saying that the word "ila" here does not mean the particle of transitivity but the singular of blessings, we say: "ila" according to this view would be a name for the reality that is truly a blessing, so according to this, the realization of the name of this word is satisfied by any part of a blessing, however small and insignificant it may be. But the people of reward, in all the stations of the Resurrection, are in complete great blessings. And one in such a condition, how can he be given good news that he will be awaiting something which is called a blessing? An example of this: a sultan of the earth gives good news that your state of greatness and power will become such after a year that you will be awaiting the obtaining of a single morsel of bread and a single drop of water. Just as that statement is corrupt, so is this.

The second position: Grant that looking transitive by the particle "ila" and joined with faces came in the language in the sense of waiting. Yet it is not possible to take this verse in that sense, because the pleasure of waiting with certainty of occurrence was already present in this world. Therefore something greater than it must be present in the Hereafter, so that its mention may be appropriate in the context of encouragement toward the Hereafter. And it is not permissible that this be merely the nearness of attainment, because that is known by reason. Thus what they mentioned of interpretation is invalidated.

The second interpretation, namely that the meaning is "to the reward of their Lord they look," is a departure from the apparent sense. As for his statement that we resorted to it because of the rational and transmitted proofs establishing that God cannot be seen, we say: we have already demonstrated in the books of rational theology the weakness of those arguments, so there is no need to mention them here. And God knows best.

They said: We only went to this interpretation because when the textual and rational proofs indicated that seeing Him, exalted is He, is impossible, it became necessary to resort to interpretation. And one might say: This verse also indicates that looking is not an expression for turning the pupil, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will not look at them﴾, and it is not meant that He turns the pupil toward Hell. If you say: What is meant is that He will not look at them with a look of mercy, that would be our answer to what they have said.

The third interpretation: that the meaning of ﴿Looking toward their Lord﴾ is that they do not ask or desire except from God. This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Worship God as if you see Him." So the people of the Resurrection, because of their intense supplication to Him and the severing of their hopes from anything else, become as if they are looking at Him. The answer: His saying: "Looking is not an expression for seeing." We say: Here there are two positions:

The first: to establish the proof that looking is seeing, in two ways:

The first: what God, exalted is He, related about Moses, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Show me [Yourself], that I may look at You﴾ (Al-A'raf: 143). If looking were an expression for turning the pupil toward the direction of the object seen, the verse would imply that Moses, peace be upon him, attributed to God, exalted is He, a direction and a place, and that is impossible.

The second: that He made looking something dependent upon desire (al-irada), so looking comes after desire. Turning the pupil does not come after desire, so it must be that looking is an expression for turning the pupil toward the direction of the object seen.

* * *

The second position, which is closer to the correct: Granting that looking is an expression for turning the pupil toward the object seen seeking to see it, we still say: since it is impossible to take it in its literal sense, it must be taken as referring to its cause, which is seeing, by using the name of the cause for the effect. Taking it to mean seeing is better than taking it to mean waiting, because turning the pupil is like a cause of seeing, and there is no connection between it and waiting. So taking it to mean seeing is better than taking it to mean waiting.

As for his saying that looking has come in the sense of waiting, we say: we have two positions in answer:

The first: that looking in the sense of waiting occurs frequently in the Qur'an, but it was never joined at all with the particle "ila," such as His saying: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾ (Al-Hadid: 13), and His saying: ﴿Do they await except its interpretation?﴾ (Al-A'raf: 53), ﴿Do they await except that God come to them?﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 210). What we claim is that looking joined with the particle "ila" and transitive to faces is nothing but in the sense of seeing or in the sense that results in seeing, which is evident. Therefore it must not occur in the sense of waiting, in order to avoid homonymy.

As for the saying of the poet:

Faces looking, on the Day of Badr, toward the Merciful, awaiting deliverance.

We say: this verse is fabricated, and the correct transmission is:

Faces looking, on the Day of Bakr, toward the Merciful, awaiting deliverance.

What is meant by this "Merciful" is Musaylimah the Liar, for they used to call him "the Merciful of Yamamah." So his companions were looking at him and expecting from him deliverance from the enemies.

As for the poet's saying:

And when I look to you from a king,

the answer is that his saying "and when I look to you" cannot mean waiting, because mere waiting does not result in a gift. Rather, what is meant by his saying "and when I look to you" is "and when I ask you," because looking at a person is the prelude to conversation, so it is permissible to express it by that. As for his saying that the word "ila" here does not mean the particle of transitivity but the singular of blessings, we say: "ila" according to this view would be a name for the reality that is truly a blessing, so according to this, the realization of the name of this word is satisfied by any part of a blessing, however small and insignificant it may be. But the people of reward, in all the stations of the Resurrection, are in complete great blessings. And one in such a condition, how can he be given good news that he will be awaiting something which is called a blessing? An example of this: a sultan of the earth gives good news that your state of greatness and power will become such after a year that you will be awaiting the obtaining of a single morsel of bread and a single drop of water. Just as that statement is corrupt, so is this.

The second position: Grant that looking transitive by the particle "ila" and joined with faces came in the language in the sense of waiting. Yet it is not possible to take this verse in that sense, because the pleasure of waiting with certainty of occurrence was already present in this world. Therefore something greater than it must be present in the Hereafter, so that its mention may be appropriate in the context of encouragement toward the Hereafter. And it is not permissible that this be merely the nearness of attainment, because that is known by reason. Thus what they mentioned of interpretation is invalidated.

The second interpretation, namely that the meaning is "to the reward of their Lord they look," is a departure from the apparent sense. As for his statement that we resorted to it because of the rational and transmitted proofs establishing that God cannot be seen, we say: we have already demonstrated in the books of rational theology the weakness of those arguments, so there is no need to mention them here. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 75, verse 24–25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And faces that Day will be bleak﴾ ﴿expecting that a calamity will be inflicted upon them.﴾ Al-basir (bleak): one who is extremely scowling. Al-basil is stronger than it, but it has come to be used for the brave when his grimness intensifies. The meaning is: they are frowning and grim-faced, their colours darkened and the traces of joy and blessing have vanished from them, because of the wretchedness and despair of Allah's mercy that has overtaken them, and because Allah has blackened them when Allah distinguishes the people of Paradise from the people of the Fire. The explanation of al-busur (bleakness) has already been given at His saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾. They were described with this attribute because they have become certain that the punishment is descending, and this is His saying: ﴿expecting that a calamity will be inflicted upon them.﴾ Here al-zann (expecting) carries the meaning of certainty (yaqin), as the exegetes have said. However, in my view, the word al-zann is mentioned here by way of mockery (tahakkum), as if it were said: when they witness those states, a suspicion arises within them that the Resurrection is true. As for al-faqirah (calamity), Abu 'Ubayda said: al-faqirah is the great calamity, and it is the name for the branding by which a mark is made on the nose. Al-Asma'i said: al-faqr is that the nose of a camel is cut until it reaches the bone, or near it, then a piece of wood is placed in it by which the camel is led. From this it is said: "al-faqirah has done its work on him." Al-Mubarrad said: al-faqirah is a calamity that breaks the back, and its origin is from al-fiqrah and al-fiqarah, as if al-faqirah is a calamity that breaks the vertebrae of the back. Ibn Qutayba said: it is said "faqartu al-rajul," just as it is said "ra'istuhu" and "batantuhu," so he is "maqfur." Know that among the exegetes are those who explained al-faqirah as the various kinds of punishment in the Fire, and al-Kalbi explained it, saying: al-faqirah is that they will be veiled from seeing their Lord and will not look at Him.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 75, verse 26:**

Allah's words, ﴿Nay!﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Kalla" is a deterrent from preferring this world over the Hereafter, as if it were said: "Since you have recognized the attribute of the happiness of the happy and the wretchedness of the wretched in the Hereafter, and you know that there is no comparison between it and this world, then refrain from preferring this world over the Hereafter, and take heed of the death that lies before you, at which the immediate life is cut off from you and you move to the deferred life, in which you will remain forever." Others said: ﴿Nay!﴾ means: "Truly, when it reaches the collarbones, such and such will happen." The intended meaning is that when He had explained the greatness of the states of the Hereafter, He explained that this world must inevitably come to an end and perish, and that one must arrive at tasting the bitterness of death. Muqatil said: ﴿Nay!﴾ means: the disbeliever does not believe in what was mentioned about the Resurrection, but he cannot repel the fact that death is inevitable, and the tasting of its pains and the bearing of its calamities.

Then Allah described that state in which the soul departs from the body, saying: ﴿When it reaches the collarbones﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** The intended meaning is "when the soul (nafs) or the spirit (ruh) reaches [the collarbones]." He reported about something that has not been previously mentioned, because the listener already knows it, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾ [al-Qadr 97:1]. The *taraqi* (collarbones) is the plural of *tarquwa*, a bone that connects the hollow of the throat with the shoulder on both sides.

Know that the reaching of the soul to the collarbones is used as a metaphor (kinaya) for being close to death. From this is the saying of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

*"And many a great affair have I warded off, when their souls had reached the collarbones."*

Its parallel is His words: ﴿Why then, when it reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:83].

**The second issue:** Some critics said: The soul reaches the collarbones only after it has departed from the heart, and once the soul has departed from the heart, death occurs without doubt. But the verse indicates that when it reaches the collarbones, life still remains, so that it can be said concerning it, "Is there any healer?" and "the shank is entwined with the shank" [al-Qiyama 75:27–29]. The answer: The meaning of His words, ﴿Nay! When it reaches the collarbones﴾, is: when closeness to that state has occurred.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 75, verses 27–29:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it will be said, "Who is a healer?"﴾ Concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: concerning "rāq" (healer) there are two interpretations.

The first: that it derives from ruqyah (spiritual incantation), as one says: "raqāhu yarqīhi ruqyah" (he recited over him), when he sought protection for him with that which heals, just as one says: "Bismillah, arqīka" (In the name of God, I recite over you). The speakers of this statement according to this interpretation are those who stand around the person near death. Then this interrogative may be understood as a request, as if they were asking for a physician to cure him and a healer to recite over him. It may also be understood as an interrogative of denial, as a person says in despair: "Who is able to recite over this person who is near death?"

The second interpretation: that His saying "man rāq" (who is a healer) derives from raqiya yarqā ruqiyyan (to ascend), and from it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Nor will we believe in your ascending﴾ [al-Isra' 93]. According to this interpretation, the speakers of this statement are the angels. Ibn 'Abbas said: The angels dislike proximity to the disbeliever, so the Angel of Death says: "Who will ascend with this disbeliever?" Al-Kalbi said: Seven angels of mercy and seven angels of punishment attend the servant at death, along with the Angel of Death. When the soul of the servant reaches the collarbones (al-tarāqī), they look at one another, each asking which of them will ascend with his spirit to heaven; so it is ﴿Who is a healer?﴾.

The second issue: Al-Wahidi said: The clear pronunciation of the nun before throat letters (ḥurūf al-fam) is good, so it is not permissible to clearly pronounce the nun of "man" in His saying ﴿man rāq﴾. Ḥafs related from 'Asim the clear pronunciation of the nun in His saying ﴿man rāq﴾ and ﴿bal rān﴾. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: I do not know the reason for this. Al-Wahidi said: The reasoning is that it may be said: the intention was to pause on "man" and "bal," so he articulated them, then began with what followed them; but this is not an accepted recitation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he thought that it was the parting﴾. The exegetes said: The meaning is that he became certain of separation from the world. Perhaps it is called certainty here "thought" because as long as the soul remains attached to its body, the person hopes for life, due to his intense love for this hasty life, as He said: ﴿No! Rather, you love the hasty life﴾; and his hope is not cut off from it, so the certainty of death does not arise for him, rather the predominant assumption (al-ẓann al-ghālib) remains together with hope for life. Or perhaps He called it "thought" by way of mockery (tahakkum).

Know that the verse indicates that the soul is a substance subsisting in itself, persisting after the death of the body, because He, the Exalted, called death "parting" (firāq), and parting only occurs if the soul remains, for parting and joining are attributes, and an attribute requires the existence of the thing it describes.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the leg is wound with the leg﴾. Iltifāf (being wound) is gathering together, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿We will bring you together as a mixed multitude﴾ [al-Isra' 104]. Concerning "al-sāq" (the leg/the severe matter) there are two statements.

The first statement: that it means the severe matter. The people of meanings said: Because when a person is overtaken by a hardship, he rolls up his leg (shammara 'an sāqihi) for it, so the severe matter is called "sāq." The Arabs say: "The war stood upon a leg," meaning it became fierce. Al-Ju'di said:

A brother of war, when war bites him it bites him, and when war rolls up its leg, he rolls up.

Then he said: The meaning of His saying ﴿And the leg is wound with the leg﴾ is: the severity of departing from the world and its pleasures and the severity of going away is wound together; or the severity of leaving family, leaving children, leaving wealth, leaving status, and the severity of the mockery of enemies and the grief of friends are wound together. In sum, the hardships there are many, such as the severity of going to the Hereafter and coming before God, or the severity of leaving loved ones and allies, and the severity of going to the house of strangeness.

The second statement: that by "sāq" is meant this specific limb. Then they mentioned several interpretations on this statement:

One: al-Sha'bi and Qatadah said: They are his two legs at death; do you not see him in the agony of death, how he strikes one leg upon the other?

Second: al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: They are his two legs when they are wound together in the shroud.

Third: that when he dies his legs become stiff, and one of them sticks to the other.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 75, verses 34–36:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Woe to you, and woe again!﴾ ﴿Then woe to you, and woe again!﴾ Qatada, al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of the hand of Abu Jahl, then said: ﴿Woe to you, and woe again!﴾ He was threatening him. Abu Jahl said: 'With what do you threaten me? Neither you nor your Lord can do anything to me. Indeed I am the most honoured person of this valley.' Then he slipped away, departing. So Allah the Exalted revealed what the Messenger, peace be upon him, had said."

The meaning of His words ﴿Awla laka﴾ is the same as "woe to you" (wayl laka), and it is a curse upon him that what he dislikes should befall him. The judge (al-Qadi) said: the meaning is "after that, distance (fa-bu'dan) for you in the matter of your worldly life, and distance for you in the matter of your afterlife." Others said: the meaning is: woe to you, once more after that.

Al-Qaffal said: this admits of several aspects:

The first: that it is a threat initiated by Allah against the disbelievers.

The second: that it is something the Prophet ﷺ said to his enemy, and the enemy of Allah found it objectionable because of his self-regard for his own might, so Allah the Exalted revealed the like of it.

The third: that this is a command from Allah to His Prophet, that he should say it to the enemy of Allah. The meaning would then be: ﴿Then he went back to his folk, swaggering﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33], so say to him, O Muhammad: ﴿Awla laka fa-awla﴾, that is, beware, for what you cannot withstand of harm has drawn near to you.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ That is: unattended, not commanded nor forbidden, not obligated in this world and not held accountable for his deeds in the Hereafter. Al-suda in the language means "neglected"; it is said: asdaytu ibili isda'an, meaning I left my camels unattended.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned at the beginning of the surah His words ﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾, He repeated that at the end of the surah, and mentioned two proofs for the soundness of the resurrection and the Last Day:

The first: His words ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ Its parallel is His words ﴿Indeed the Hour is coming; I am almost concealing it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], and His words ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ Its explanation: that granting capability, instruments and reason without obligation and without command to obey and prohibition from corruptions implies that He, exalted is He, is pleased with ugly deeds, and that is not befitting to His wisdom. Therefore obligation is necessary, and obligation is not fitting or becoming for the Generous, the Merciful, unless there is an abode of reward, resurrection and the Last Day.

Then He explained them, saying: ﴿the male and the female﴾. ﴿Is not that One able to give life to the dead?﴾ The meaning: Is not He who originated these things able to re-create? It is related that when the Prophet ﷺ recited it, he would say: "Glory be to You, yes, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." And may His blessings be upon our master Muhammad, the master of the messengers, and upon his family and companions, and may He grant them peace.

The second proof for the validity of the doctrine of resurrection: arguing from the first creation to the re-creation. This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿Did He not used to be a drop of semen emitted?﴿ (Qur'an 75:37). There are two issues here.

First issue: the nutfah (drop) is a small quantity of water, its plural being nitaf and nutaf. He says: Was he not a little water in the loins of the man and the breastbones of the woman? His saying, ﴿of semen emitted﴾, means that it is poured into the womb. We have discussed the matter of yumna (emitted) at His saying, ﴿from a drop when it is emitted﴾ and His saying, ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ (Qur'an 56:58). If it is asked: what is the benefit of yumna in His saying, ﴿of semen emitted﴾? We say: it contains an indication of the lowliness of his state, as if it were said: he is created from semen that passed through the place of impurity, so it is not fitting for such a thing to rebel against the obedience of Allah the Exalted. However, He expressed this meaning by way of allusion, as in His saying, the Exalted, concerning Jesus and Mary: ﴿They used to eat food﴾ (Qur'an 5:75), and what is meant by it is the relieving of a need.

Second issue: regarding yumna in this surah there are two readings, with the letter ta and with the letter ya. The ta refers to the nutfah, on the reckoning: Was he not a drop emitted from semen? The ya refers to the semen in "semen emitted," meaning: the creation of man is measured from it.
